title: LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN
description: Preserve unmatched records using outer joins, find missing associations with anti-joins, and master ON vs WHERE placement.

data.text: A **`LEFT OUTER JOIN`** (or simply `LEFT JOIN`) returns all records from the left table, along with matching rows from the right table. If no match exists, NULL values are filled in for all right-table columns. Conversely, `RIGHT JOIN` preserves all rows from the right table (though industry convention strongly prefers rewriting `RIGHT JOIN` as `LEFT JOIN`).
The Critical Anti-Join Pattern (Finding Unmatched Rows)

An **Anti-Join** identifies rows in the left table that have NO corresponding records in the right table (e.g. finding users who have never placed an order). This is accomplished with `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right_table.id IS NULL`.

data.title: Finding Inactive Users via Anti-Join
data.content: High-performance search for customers with zero orders.
data.code:
SELECT 
    c.id AS customer_id,
    c.email,
    c.created_at
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o 
    ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL -- Excludes any customer with matching orders!
ORDER BY c.created_at DESC;

data.title: The `ON` vs `WHERE` Trap in LEFT JOIN
data.text: In a `LEFT JOIN`, filtering the right table in the `WHERE` clause (e.g. `WHERE o.status = 'ACTIVE'`) converts your query into an `INNER JOIN` because NULLs fail the filter! Always place right-table conditions inside the `ON` clause to preserve unmatched left rows.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `LEFT JOIN` preserves all rows from the left table, filling missing right-side data with `NULL`.
Use the Anti-Join pattern (`WHERE right.id IS NULL`) to detect orphan or inactive records.
Filters on the right table must stay in the `ON` clause to avoid accidentally turning a `LEFT JOIN` into an `INNER JOIN`.
